newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-Philippines fights another attack on peso.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Philippines fights another attack on peso.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank defended the peso against a fresh attack on Monday, raising its key money market rate to two-year highs after foreign exchange intervention failed to keep speculators at bay.

The central bank raised its key overnight lending rate by six percentage points to 30 percent -- which compares with just 15 percent before Southeast Asian markets were roiled by the baht's defacto devaluation last Wednesday.
The peso kept its poise, and was quoted by traders at 26.40 to the dollar after the central bank sold the U.S. currency at that level. This was only slightly weaker than 26.399 previously.

Finance secretary Roberto de Ocampo swiftly denied a Singapore newspaper report which triggered fresh speculation against the peso by quoting him as saying the Philippine currency may be officially devalued against the U.S. dollar.
"The (level of) the Philippine peso is based on market forces and not determined by the government," De Ocampo said.
"The Philippines will not resort to any shift in policy to a fixed rate system that saw a downfall of the financial system in Mexico two years ago and in Thailand just recently."
The story, carried by the Singapore Sunday Times, had a banner headline which read "Philippine peso may devalue against U.S.$" but had no direct devaluation quote from De Ocampo.
But it quoted him as saying the peso's decline "will be gradual and not dramatic, in which case there will be a balance of benefits".
In a separate statement, Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said there would be no change in foreign exchange policy.
"(The rate) shall not be administratively fixed but shall be determined through transactions in the foreign exchange market on a day-to-day basis," he said.

Analysts have warned the peso may be one of the next Asian currencies to slide in the aftermath of the baht crisis because of the country's swollen current account deficit and overheated property sector.
Philippine businessmen have repeatedly urged the government to allow the peso to depreciate in order to make their exports more competitive.
The Central Bank freed up foreign exchange regulations in 1992, and intervenes by buying or selling dollars when it wants to influence the level of the peso.

On Monday, it raised its offer rate for one-day reverse repurchase agreements -- effectively the overnight rate -- to 30 percent, up sharply from 24 percent last week. The last time the Central Bank raised this rate to 30 percent was in March 1995 in the wake of Mexico's financial crisis.
Many analysts believe there is no reason for the peso to follow in the baht's footsteps.

"The peso has adjusted more than the baht compared to the last five years. The peso is not overvalued compared to the baht," said Rolando Valuenzuela, senior vice president of Philippine TA Securities.
"We have been adjusting consistently with inflation, growth and the balance of payments," he said.
There was no fundamental pressure for the peso to depreciate, he said, citing the country's low inflation and strong exports.
